title: Zhuangzi’s Perspective-Skepticism — no view from nowhere
when: The text’s earliest strata are generally placed in China’s Warring States period (roughly 4th–3rd centuries BCE). Zhuang Zhou is usually dated to the latter 4th century BCE, though the received Zhuangzi is a composite anthology edited into its present 33 chapters by Guo Xiang around the early 4th century CE; authorship and dating of individual chapters remain debated.
people: Zhuang Zhou (Zhuangzi); Hui Shi; later editor-commentator Guo Xiang
origin: Classical Chinese philosophy, especially the intellectual debates of the Warring States period.
idea: In the Zhuangzi’s second chapter, familiar distinctions—right and wrong, this and that—are shown to depend partly on the standpoint and standards from which people judge. The text does not simply conclude that all claims are equally true or that reasoning is useless. Instead, its shifting dialogues and parables unsettle confidence that any speaker possesses a complete, context-free vantage point. Our judgments remain necessary for living and choosing, but they can be limited, revisable, and entangled with our habits and circumstances. The famous dream of Zhuang Zhou as a butterfly dramatizes this instability of perspective, although the text’s broader argument is not reducible to that single story. Scholars disagree about how skeptical or relativist to make the position, and the anthology’s different layers should not be treated as one author’s perfectly uniform doctrine.
relevance: In polarized public debate and algorithmically tailored media, the Zhuangzi offers a demanding form of intellectual humility: examine the standpoint behind a confident judgment, without pretending that every perspective is equally informed or abandoning practical decision-making.
